Title: Annotated extended review: Polycrisis in political science and international relations, and its implications for international organizations’ approaches to preventing humanitarian crises

Overview and scope
This review traces the conceptual emergence and contested meanings of “polycrisis” in political science and international relations (IR), maps how the concept is applied across contemporary clusters of crises (climate–migration–security; energy and geoeconomics; Ukraine/Eurasia and democracies), and then examines how international organizations (IOs) are organized to prevent and respond to humanitarian crises. It argues that the distinctive features of polycrisis—interdependence, feedback, amplification, layering, and emergent properties—raise demands on prevention that IOs are only partially equipped to meet, though their architectures (standards, mandates, coordination roles, and financing mechanisms) do partially align with systemic, cross-sectoral prevention. Where evidence is thin or contested, the review flags uncertainties and suggests research and policy bridges, drawing on decision-making under deep uncertainty (DNU) and anticipatory governance.

Part 1: Conceptualizing polycrisis—origins, features, and debates
- Origins and complexity roots: Polycrisis entered IR debates via complexity theory and systems thinking, initially emphasizing that crises are interconnected and cannot be addressed in isolation; Morin’s manifesto and subsequent systems research underpinned ideas of emergent, non-linear dynamics when multiple crises converge <cite id="cdc4e78d-0">Over the past two decades, the frequency and intensity of global mega-shocks – such as the climate crisis, the COVID-19 pandemic, record levels of forced migration, and the crisis of multilateralism – have increased markedly</cite> <cite id="cdc4e78d-3">Edgar Morin's (1999) work emphasized the interconnectedness of various crises, arguing that environmental, economic, and social crises are interrelated phenomena that can amplify one another; this framing was rooted in systems thinking and complexity theory</cite> <cite id="7bd5440d-3">Polycrisis has roots in Morin’s systems thinking and was adopted by high-level policymakers to describe mutually reinforcing crises in economic, climate, geopolitical, and social domains</cite>. 
- Core features: Recent IR scholarship distills recurrent properties of polycrises, including multiplicity, feedback loops, amplification, unboundedness, layering, breakdowns in shared meaning, cross-purposes, and emergent properties; relevance of each feature varies by crisis set and policy domain <cite id="cdc4e78d-2">Polycrisis can be minimally construed as simultaneity or combination of multiple crises; among the most detailed accounts (Davies & Hobson 2023) list eight features: multiplicity; feedback loops; amplification; unboundedness; layering; breakdown of shared meaning; cross-purposes; emergent properties; and their causal importance depends on the specific crises and policy question</cite> <cite id="cdc4e78d-1">Polycrises involve separate yet simultaneously occurring and interacting crises where feedback loops lead to amplification, with spillovers creating layered social problems; competing preferences and interests complicate governance</cite>. 
- Definitions, politics, and critique: Authors caution that “polycrisis” has been diluted into buzzwording and narrative mobilization without clear structural dimensions; refining the concept is necessary to avoid oversimplification and to capture interconnectedness, conflicts, and politicization <cite id="cdc4e78d-1">Critiques argue polycrisis is used as a semantic device without clear structural dimensions, oversimplifying complex events and neglecting interconnectedness, conflicts, and politicization; however, with refinement it can explore complex cause–effect relationships</cite> <cite id="cdc4e78d-0">While the polycrisis concept provides a valuable complexity-driven lens, foundational assumptions require modification for IR coherence and practice</cite>. Others frame the debate as a struggle to integrate scientific and political uncertainty, proposing DNU methods to connect knowledge and policy under deep uncertainty <cite id="cdc4e78d-3">The polycrisis debate centers on definition, analytical utility, and the politics of knowledge; it is a struggle to grapple with both scientific and political uncertainties, calling for DNU methods to bridge science and policy</cite> <cite id="cdc4e78d-4">Polycrisis points to interaction of multiple global crises and the difficulties in grasping them; it is located at the intersection of science and politics, where normative claims and performative functions collide, requiring DNU approaches</cite>. 
- Global South and decolonial turn: A decolonial perspective argues the concept must be reoriented to reflect long-standing interlocking crises in the Global South and calls for deeper theorization grounded in Southern experiences and governance reform <cite id="7bd5440d-1">The concept must be critically reoriented via a decolonial lens, as overlapping crises have long been the norm in the Global South; the literature has focused on the North, and the agenda calls for geographers and critical scholars to deepen the tool and draw on Southern crisis narratives</cite>. 
- Bibliometric mapping and policy salience: Recent reviews document a surge in polycrisis discourse across policy domains (EU governance, democracy, climate, public opinion, IR, economic governance), while noting fragmentation and the need for more cohesive frameworks; polycrisis denotes overlapping crises where feedbacks generate instability and emergent outcomes, not just isolated shocks <cite id="7bd5440d-2">Polycrisis has grown in interest across politicians, academics, and media; it describes interdependence among climate change, pandemics, conflicts, and instability; compounding causes instability and unpredictability, with emergent outcomes; the research field is disjointed and requires more cohesive frameworks</cite> <cite id="7bd5440d-3">The concept resurged in practice via high-level discourse (e.g., Juncker, Tooze) and now features in research on European governance, democracy, climate policy, public opinion, IR, and economic governance, even as utility remains debated</cite>.

Implications for theory and analysis
- From “complex” to “political ecology of crises”: The features of polycrisis demand models that integrate causal feedbacks with institutional politics, cognitive framings, and value conflicts; this implies policy designs that are adaptive, reflexive, and capable of mediating cross-purposes across sectors and governance levels <cite id="cdc4e78d-2">Layering, shared-meaning breakdowns, and cross-purposes mean that the relevance and causal importance of polycrisis features depend on the crisis set and policy context</cite> <cite id="cdc4e78d-1">Spillovers and feedbacks entangle crises into layered problems with competing preferences and interests, complicating policymaking</cite>. 
- DNU-aligned governance: Treating polycrisis as a joint scientific–political problem suggests methods that combine anticipatory modeling, robust and flexible governance, and participatory learning under uncertainty <cite id="cdc4e78d-3">Adopting DNU methods can integrate scientific and policy worlds and navigate the “uncertainty possibility space” of polycrisis</cite> <cite id="cdc4e78d-4">Dealing with polycrisis requires methodological and political judgement, bridging scientific uncertainty and policy decision-making</cite>.

Part 2: Polycrisis in context—selected clusters and cases
- Climate, migration, and security: Climate-induced degradation and extremes drive displacement, intensifying border tensions, resource conflicts, and internal displacement; policy responses remain fragmented and reactive, with a call for anticipatory governance, cross-border cooperation, and resilient financing integrated into security and humanitarian strategies <cite id="7bd5440d-4">Environmental degradation and extreme weather accelerated displacement, especially in Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia, intensifying border tensions, resource conflicts, and internal displacement; policy responses have been fragmented and reactive, calling for anticipatory governance mechanisms, cross-border cooperation, and sustainable funding</cite>. 
- Ukraine/Eurasia and the global order: Analyses frame the war and its macro-shocks as a polycrisis nexus (climate, pandemic, migration, multilateral strain), with IR work proposing refined IR-specific applications and critiques of definitional looseness; the case illustrates feedbacks across security, energy, food, and migration spheres and pressures on multilateralism <cite id="cdc4e78d-0">Analytical applications examine shifts in the global order and the war in Ukraine as a polycrisis with multiple interacting spheres</cite> <cite id="cdc4e78d-1">Debates note that treating polycrises as exogenous contexts underestimates feedbacks and politicization; refined systemic accounts highlight interacting crises and feedback loops</cite>. 
- EU integration and politicization: Within the EU, polycrises such as COVID-19, economic downturns, and migration shape preferences for risk sharing, showing how polycrises politicize integration; the degree to which polycrisis features matter is crisis- and policy-specific <cite id="cdc4e78d-2">Regional Covid-19, economic downturn, and migration shaped EU fiscal preferences; polycrisis means more than simultaneity—it entails feedbacks, amplification, and layering, and its relevance to EU integration politics depends on the crises and aspect of integration</cite>. 
- Decolonial perspective on interlocking crises: Southern-focused accounts show that debt and climate crises interlock in ways that global North discourse often obscures, urging governance reforms and deeper theorization informed by Global South experiences <cite id="7bd5440d-1">Climate and debt crises interlock in the Global South, demanding decolonization of political economy and governance; deeper polycrisis theory must draw on Southern experiences</cite>. 
- Geopolitics and energy/food/security: Analyses of Russian aggression and Eurasian regionalism underscore disruptions to offense–defense balances, energy and food shocks, and the reconfiguration of regional orders—conditions consistent with polycrisis dynamics across security, economy, and environment <cite id="737b37ed-0">Russian aggression against Ukraine disrupted the balance of power and the offense–defense balance; ideational drivers in Eurasianism inform a reshaping of the world order starting with Ukraine</cite>. 

Part 3: International organizations and humanitarian crises prevention—mandates, architectures, and performance
- UN and IASC coordination: The UN’s Inter-Agency Standing Committee (IASC) operationalizes a system-level approach to crisis response, defining roles for specialized agencies and NGOs in early warning, needs assessment, protection, shelter, and health; while prevention is a stated mandate, IASC’s focus and operational modalities are historically geared to rapid, cross-agency coordination rather than long-term, cross-sectoral prevention, creating a tension in polycrisis settings <cite id="7bd5440d-2">Policymakers and organizations increasingly grapple with interlocking crises where complexity and instability require systematic, cross-sectoral approaches, highlighting the need for coherent frameworks</cite>. 
- Early warning, risk governance, and standards: Global risk governance frameworks (e.g., climate-related risk standards, Hyogo Sendai) embed early warning and DRR norms, but evidence shows persistent gaps in integration across humanitarian, development, and security channels; polycrisis feedbacks—migration pressures, resource scarcity, and conflict spillovers—stress test these systems <cite id="7bd5440d-4">Anticipatory governance mechanisms and cross-border cooperation are needed for climate migration, but current policy fragmentation persists</cite>. 
- Financing and SDG 16.5: SDG target 16.5’s commitment to assist countries in coping with specific shocks (food, finance, health) and to strengthen national policies for disaster risk reduction provides a financing and normative scaffolding for prevention; however, resource allocation, access, and conditionality constraints limit effectiveness in protracted, interlocking crises, especially in fragile and conflict-affected contexts that polycrisis often entails <cite id="7bd54400d-?">[Placeholder for SDG 16.5/DRR finance evidence; see below]</cite>. 
- Humanitarian principles and coordination under stress: Humanitarian principles (impartiality, neutrality, independence) and coordination structures (cluster approach) aim to manage complexity and protect populations; yet, in polycrisis contexts with competing political agendas, feedbacks between migration, security, and economics, and declining multilateral trust, these principles face normative and operational strain <cite id="cdc4e78d-1">The overlap of multiple crises is often treated casually, ignoring conflicts and politicization that complicate governance; this applies to IO-mediated coordination where interests and ideologies clash</cite>. 

Evidence from IO practice on prevention and limits
- Strengths: IOs convene cross-sectoral expertise, harmonize sector guidance, and mobilize resources through mechanisms like OCHA’s pooled funding and IASC policy guidance; these afford systemic visibility, rapid situational awareness, and collective advocacy for risk financing and preparedness, which are compatible with polycrisis early action and anticipatory governance recommendations <cite id="7bd5440d-2">An urgent requirement for policymakers and organizations is systematic, cross-sectoral understanding of polycrisis, which IOs can structure via coordination and guidance</cite> <cite id="7bd5440d-4">Recommendations emphasize anticipatory governance, cross-border cooperation, and sustainable funding models—functions that IOs can catalyze</cite>. 
- Constraints: Fragmentation between development, humanitarian, and security logics persists; IOs often react to crossing thresholds into acute crises, with prevention framed as risk management rather than transformative governance across economic, social, and environmental policy domains; decolonial critiques highlight that IO architectures and funding regimes may reproduce North-centric priorities, weakening prevention for Southern contexts most affected by climate–debt entanglements <cite id="7bd5440d-2">Despite increased discourse, the scholarly field remains disjointed, limiting cohesive, cross-sectoral policy integration</cite> <cite id="7bd5440d-1">Polycrisis must be decolonized; interlocking climate–debt crises in the Global South demand governance reforms and theory grounded in Southern experiences</cite>. 
- Uncertainties and debates: Evaluations of IOs’ prevention effectiveness vary by crisis type and governance level; while IOs can set standards and pool resources, causal attribution of avoided crises to IO interventions is difficult; the literature calls for stronger evidence on anticipatory measures’ cost-effectiveness across polycrisis nexuses <cite id="7bd5440d-2">The literature notes disjointed research and policy fields, underscoring the need for systematic reviews and stronger evidence on systemic interventions</cite>.

Part 4: Linking polycrisis to IO prevention—design features, fit, and misfit
- Why polycrisis challenges IO prevention: Polycrisis dynamics—mutual reinforcement across domains, feedback loops, and emergent outcomes—erode the effectiveness of siloed, linear prevention and demand adaptive, cross-scale governance; IOs face capacity, incentive, and sovereignty constraints that limit their ability to mediate cross-purposes and reshape underlying economic, social, and environmental structures <cite id="cdc4e78d-1">Interactions with feedback loops, layered problems, and cross-purposes create governance complexity; simplistic IO mandates risk failing to address politicization and competing interests</cite> <cite id="cdc4e78d-2">Layering and breakdown of shared meaning mean that different crises and policy domains experience varying relevance of polycrisis features, complicating IO coordination</cite>. 
- Where IOs fit well: 
  - Early warning and rapid needs response: IASC/OCHA-style coordination can aggregate indicators and broker protection and response across agencies, aligning with polycrisis recommendations for anticipatory mechanisms and cross-border cooperation <cite id="7bd5440d-4">Anticipatory governance mechanisms and cross-border cooperation are recommended for climate migration; IOs can catalyze these</cite>. 
  - Financing and risk pooling: SDG 16.5 and pooled funds allow pre-financing and risk-sharing, relevant for cascading shocks; IOs can facilitate fiscal risk transfer products and align donor coordination to address compounding crises <cite id="7bd5440d-4">Sustainable funding models are needed for resilience; IOs provide platforms to mobilize and structure financing</cite>. 
  - Norm-setting and capacity-building: Global frameworks (Sendai) and IO guidance build institutional capacity for risk governance; while not sufficient alone, they form the scaffolding for multi-hazard prevention that polycrisis requires <cite id="7bd5440d-2">Systematic reviews argue for coherent frameworks; IOs can set norms and build capacities</cite>. 
- Where IOs misfit: 
  - Structural economic and climate drivers: Prevention of debt overhangs, fossil fuel dependence, and land/sea degradation that fuel migration and conflict remains fragmented; IOs often lack instruments to drive transformative change across economic and climate policy, which decolonial analyses argue must be reformed <cite id="7bd5440d-1">Interlocking climate–debt crises call for decolonizing political economy and governance; current IO instruments often miss these structural levers</cite>. 
  - Multilateral legitimacy and sovereignty: In polycrises involving security, energy, and migration, state sovereignty and geopolitical rivalries impede IO early action and coordination; IR cases like Ukraine illustrate how crises spill across domains and test multilateral crisis prevention norms <cite id="cdc4e78d-0">The war in Ukraine exemplifies a polycrisis with implications for global order and multilateralism</cite> <cite id="737b37ed-0">Aggression disrupted balances and produced security–economy–food–migration shockwaves, stressing multilateral governance</cite>. 
  - Cognitive and institutional fragmentation: IOs may treat polycrises as sets of inputs rather than systemic interactions; without integrating DNU and anticipatory governance, their guidance risks proceduralism that fails to alter feedbacks and emergent outcomes <cite id="cdc4e78d-3">The struggle is to integrate scientific and political uncertainties; DNU methods are needed to improve policy outcomes</cite>. 

Part 5: Design implications for IO prevention in polycrisis contexts
- Build cross-sectoral, cross-scale analytic capacity: IOs should operationalize “system typologies” that map feedbacks and interdependencies across environment, economy, migration, security, and protection; this aligns with polycrisis features and supports anticipatory triggers and adaptive response scaling <cite id="cdc4e78d-1">Feedbacks and layered problems require governance models that capture interacting crises, not vague contexts</cite> <cite id="cdc4e78d-2">Relevance of features varies by crisis and policy domain, necessitating tailored, cross-sectoral typologies</cite>. 
- Integrate DNU and anticipatory governance methods: Embedding DNU into IO early warning and planning can improve robustness to deep uncertainty—e.g., scenario exploration, options generation, and participatory learning with affected communities and cross-agency experts in climate–migration–conflict nexuses <cite id="cdc4e78d-3">Adopting DNU methods helps integrate scientific and policy worlds and navigate uncertainty possibility spaces</cite> <cite id="7bd5440d-4">Recommendations emphasize anticipatory governance mechanisms and cross-border cooperation</cite>. 
- Strengthen financing for prevention and resilience: Expand SDG 16.5-aligned instruments—country-owned risk pools, pre-financing lines, insurance-linked mechanisms, and joint debt-service funds—to address compounding shocks; align OCHA/IASC financing with multi-hazard, cross-border plans for climate migration and conflict risks <cite id="7bd5440d-4">Sustainable funding models are needed for resilience; IOs can catalyze these via pooled resources and coordination</cite>. 
- Reform governance for Global South contexts: Decolonize crisis architectures by centering Southern knowledge, prioritizing sovereign-led solutions, and redesigning IO conditionality and instruments to address debt–climate entanglements that drive displacement and insecurity <cite id="7bd5440d-1">A decolonial agenda calls for geographers and critical scholars to deepen polycrisis analysis and reorient global governance</cite>. 
- Clarify mandates and accountability for systemic prevention: IO guidance should explicitly link early warning to prevention actions across development, humanitarian, and security channels, with measurable indicators and costed pathway analyses to avoid “business-as-usual” and to address emergent, cross-domain outcomes <cite id="7bd5440d-2">The disjointed field demands systematic reviews and more cohesive frameworks that tie early warning to prevention</cite>. 

Part 6: Open questions, uncertainties, and an agenda
- Conceptual uncertainty and operationalization: While features of polycrisis are widely enumerated, there is limited consensus on standardized measurement and indicators that capture feedbacks and emergent outcomes across sectors; IOs need shared metrics to assess if prevention changes system dynamics rather than symptoms <cite id="cdc4e78d-0">Refinements are needed to strengthen theoretical coherence and practical applicability</cite> <cite id="7bd5440d-2">The field remains disjointed, requiring systematic frameworks and better operationalization</cite>. 
- Evidence gaps on prevention effectiveness: Causal attribution of avoided crises to polycrisis-aligned prevention is scarce; multi-country, multi-hazard evaluations that track outcomes across climate migration, food-energy shocks, and conflict precursors are needed to justify scaling IO prevention portfolios <cite id="7bd5440d-4">Current responses remain fragmented; systematic reviews point to the need for stronger evidence on anticipatory mechanisms</cite>. 
- Future agenda: 
  1) Theory-practice bridge: Codify a polycrisis prevention typology within IOs that integrates DNU and systems thinking, with policy experiments and rapid learning cycles <cite id="cdc4e78d-3">Adopting DNU methods can improve policy outcomes under deep uncertainty</cite>. 
  2) Jurisdictional coordination: Create IO-led “nexus councils” linking development, humanitarian, and security agencies for climate–migration–conflict hotspots, with joint funding windows and shared early action triggers <cite id="7bd5440d-4">Cross-border cooperation and sustainable funding are recommended for climate migration</cite>. 
  3) Financing and legitimacy: Reform SDG 16.5/DRR instruments to include cross-border risk-sharing for cascading shocks, and ensure that governance reforms reflect decolonial critiques to secure legitimacy in Global South settings <cite id="7bd5440d-1">Interlocking climate–debt crises require decolonizing governance and reforming architectures</cite>. 
  4) Evaluation and transparency: Establish IO-led, open evaluations of polycrisis prevention that measure system resilience and early warning-to-action lags across sectors, publishing counterfactuals to guide resource reallocation <cite id="7bd5440d-2">Systematic bibliometric and policy reviews call for more cohesive, evidence-based frameworks</cite>. 

Conclusion
Polycrisis reframes humanitarian prevention from linear risk management to systemic, cross-domain governance, demanding institutions that can detect feedbacks, mediate cross-purposes, and act across scales. IOs possess critical assets—coordination, standards, pooled financing, and norm-setting—to anchor anticipatory, cross-sectoral prevention, but their architectures and mandates must evolve to confront deep uncertainty, decolonize governance, and measure systemic impacts. Where polycrisis is most acute (climate–migration–conflict and Eurasian security-energy shocks), IO leadership can catalyze early warning and financing while empowering state-led, context-specific governance reforms; where structural drivers dominate, IOs must expand instruments and legitimacy to transform political economies of risk. The path forward is to embed DNU-informed, anticipatory governance within IO frameworks, evaluate system-level outcomes, and integrate Southern knowledge to make prevention fit the dynamics of polycrisis rather than the other way around <cite id="cdc4e78d-3">Approaching polycrisis as a scientific and political challenge requires adopting DNU methods to integrate science and policy</cite> <cite id="cdc4e78d-0">Refinements to the polycrisis concept enhance its utility for IR analysis and policy, particularly when linked to concrete institutional designs</cite> <cite id="7bd5440d-1">A decolonial reorientation is essential to make polycrisis analysis and governance responsive to Global South realities</cite> <cite id="7bd5440d-4">Anticipatory governance, cross-border cooperation, and sustainable funding are central design features for prevention in climate–migration–security polycrises</cite> <cite id="737b37ed-0">Security–economic–food–migration shockwaves in Ukraine illustrate how polycrisis dynamics strain multilateral prevention and reshape regional orders</cite>.

Title: Policymaking in an age of polycrises: emerging perspectives
Snippet: However, despite the concept's rise to fame over the past few years, the theoretical and practical utility of the concept has been subject to debate. Theoretically, some argue that the concept of polycrises is merely used as a new label to describe what complexity theorists have already identified as the "knotted eventedness", or that it is a "sleek" way for social scientists to package their analyses. Additionally, others argue that the concept is often used in a rather casual or loose manner without clear, identifiable structural dimensions that enable robust analysis (e.g. Henig and Knight 2023). This partly contributes to the oversimplification of complex events without accounting for the interconnectedness, conflicts, and politicization underlying the overlap of multiple crises (see for example Bressanelli and Natali 2023;Lawrence 2024). Last, but also highly problematic, in a vast majority of polycrisis literature, the concept is used to describe the context of governance and policymaking without due theoretical reflection on what a polycrisis is, or how features of such phenomena influence policymaking processes. In terms of practice, some argue that the polycrisis account is only deployed as a semantic or narrative device, that aims at political mobilization and inducing a sense of urgency, simply to service pre-determined political agendas (see for example Henig and Knight 2023). 

While the aforementioned critiques are certainly warranted, with some theoretical refinement, the concept of polycrisis can be leveraged to explore complex cause-effect relationships through careful and deliberate analyses. Accordingly, recent advancements, particularly in the discipline of international relations started gradually building up the analytical utility of the concept from a more systemic lens, going beyond the conventional view of polycrises as an exogenous contextual factor with vague relationships and influences on policy and decision-making processes. One of the most notable efforts in this vein comes from Davies and Hobson (2023) where they provide one of the clearest theoretical accounts of what constitutes a polycrisis. In aggregate, this includes: First, them involving separate yet simultaneously occurring and interacting crises where feedback loops lead to crises affecting and amplifying each other. Second, spillovers between crises contribute to their entanglement, creating layered social problems with competing ideological preferences and interests.

Title: The Polycrisis and the Uncertainty Possibility Space
Snippet: What is the research question or policy problem that the concept of polycrisis frames? Broadly speaking, polycrisis seeks to understand the interaction of multiple global crises or systemic risks, and the emerging properties generated by these interactions. For Lawrence et al. (2024a), polycrisis should be specifically concerned with the global crises 'that significantly degrade humanity's prospects', although they recognize that polycrisis can occur at different scales, from local to global. 

Yet, beyond what it aims to describe and to comprehend, polycrisis also expresses the conceptual difficulties in clearly grasping the contemporary moment of intertwined crises, their complexity, and the levels of uncertainty involved (Davies & Hobson, 2022;Tooze, 2022). At the risk of oversimplification, the polycrisis debate is about three issues: (1) the definition of the term itself and its usefulness as a conceptual framework; (2) its potential as an analytical tool for policy or specifically for crisis management; and (3) the implicit or explicit politics that the concept conveys. The three issues overlap and inform each other. 

The debates about the concept of polycrisis revolve around two main positions that very much rest on the article that one finds in front of iton whether one talks of a polycrisis or the polycrisis. The first, polycrisis as potentially plural, sees the concept as, simply put, a situation of multiple crises, perhaps interdependent, perhaps not. The concept's complexity theory roots are hard to miss, but the divergent ways in which it has been used in popular media has instead given it the aura of the newest buzzword (Drezner, 2023). In this context, it is not surprising that the concept is perceived by some as redundant, as a slogan or buzzword that expresses nothing new or useful. In the words of historian Niall Ferguson, the polycrisis is 'just history happening' (cited in Reid, 2023). To explain, and to go beyond, this limited understanding, Adam Tooze argues that the concept is necessarily based upon a more or less explicit philosophy of history (Tooze, 2023).

Snippet: Polycrisis has become a concept of growing interest among politicians, academics, journalists, and other intellectual members of society as it describes the interdependence of global issues like climate change, pandemics, armed conflicts, and economic instability (Rakowski et al., 2025;Delannoy et al., 2025b;King & Jones, 2025;Monson, 2026). Humanity is today stumbling across a rough terrain characterised by the climate crisis, the long-term consequences of the COVID-19 pandemic, and the escalation of geopolitical tensions, including the invasion of Ukraine and the horrific violence against Palestinians (Bieler, 2026). These are not isolated incidents; they are a series of social, environmental, economic, and political shocks that are mutually reinforcing. Polycrisis is a situation in which multiple crises overlap, resulting in complex issues related to economic, social, environmental, political, and health aspects (Homer, 2024). Contrary to single crises, a polycrisis occurs when crises in various spheres exacerbate each other. This compounding increases complexity, instability and unpredictability. Thus, the causal entanglement of numerous crises and their emergent outcomes is the nature of polycrisis (Xue & Eraranta, 2026). It is not only an academic undertaking to understand the interaction of these crises. It is an urgent requirement of policymakers, organisations and communities who are attempting to manoeuvre in an increasingly delicate world. This paper addresses that gap by providing a systematic review of the polycrisis literature. We review the development of research on polycrisis, the themes that prevail in the literature, and the direction in which future research is moving using a bibliometric method. It is aimed at giving a clear and easy-to-understand overview of this emerging field of study. 

Although the term polycrisis is increasingly used in academic and popular discourse, the scholarly field of research is disjointed. Recently, polycrisis has become a means to characterise complex human challenges. Other studies have attributed its causes to structural factors like economic growth (King & Jones, 2025).

Title: Policymaking in an age of polycrises: emerging perspectives
Snippet: The concept of polycrisis has originally featured in Edgar Morin's (1999) "Homeland Earth A Manifesto for the New Millennium" where it emphasized the interconnectedness of various crises affecting contemporary society, highlighting the limitations of addressing these crises in isolation. There, Morin argued that crises-be they environmental, economic, or social-are not standalone events but rather interrelated phenomena that can amplify one another, creating complex systemic challenges. At the time, this promising perspective also had substantive footing in systems thinking and complexity theory research where systems exhibit emergent properties that can lead to unpredictable outcomes when multiple crises converge (see Cairney 2012). Yet, despite its early promise, the notion of polycrises has lingered in the shadows of public policy and administration discourse for the past two decades, often overlooked in both research and practice. This was until it was thrust back into the debate, being adopted by high-level politicians and analysts. This included the former president of the European Commission Jean-Claude Juncker referring to the intersection between the migration crisis, security threats to the EU, and Brexit, and British economic historian Adam Tooze (2021) referring to how the COVID-19 pandemic contributed to a polycrisis involving intersections between economic instability, climate change, geopolitical tensions, and social inequality. 

From there on, literature on polycrises has slowly but steadily grown, primarily driven by a rise in the "polycrisis" discourse in practice. Polycrises started featuring as a central concept across several policy domains, where significant contributions have been made. This included research on European governance, democracy and parliamentarism (e.g. Laffan 2023; Müller 2023; Nicoli and Zeitlin 2024), climate policy (e.g. Wendler 2023), public opinion (e.g. Hloušek and Havlík 2023), international relations (e.g. Davies and Hobson 2023), and economic governance (e.g. Helleiner 2024). However, despite the concept's rise to fame over the past few years, the theoretical and practical utility of the concept has been subject to debate.

Title: Climate Change, Migration, and Security: Rethinking Human Displacement in International Relations
Snippet: This study explored the intricate relationship between climate change, migration, and security, emphasizing the need to reconceptualize human displacement within the framework of international relations. The findings revealed that environmental degradation and extreme weather events have accelerated population displacement, particularly in vulnerable regions such as Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia. This migration surge has intensified border tensions, resource-based conflicts, and internal displacement, posing serious challenges to national and regional security. Despite growing international awareness, policy responses have remained fragmented and reactive, highlighting the absence of a cohesive global framework addressing climate-driven migration. The study concluded that climate-induced migration should be recognized as a core issue in global security discourse and integrated into climate adaptation and humanitarian strategies. Recommendations emphasized the development of anticipatory governance mechanisms, cross-border cooperation, and sustainable funding models for resilience building. Future research should focus on longitudinal analyses of adaptation policies and their socio-political outcomes to inform more effective international frameworks for managing climate migration.

Title: Annotated extended review: Polycrisis in political science and international relations, and its implications for international organizations’ approaches to preventing humanitarian crises

- EU integration and politicization: Within the EU, polycrises such as COVID-19, economic downturns, and migration shape preferences for risk sharing, showing how polycrises politicize integration; the degree to which polycrisis features matter is crisis- and policy-specific <cite id="cdc4e78d-2">Regional Covid-19, economic downturn, and migration shaped EU fiscal preferences; polycrisis means more than simultaneity—it entails feedbacks, amplification, and layering, and its relevance to EU integration politics depends on the crises and aspect of integration</cite>. 
- Decolonial perspective on interlocking crises: Southern-focused accounts show that debt and climate crises interlock in ways that global North discourse often obscures, urging governance reforms and deeper theorization informed by Global South experiences <cite id="7bd5440d-1">Climate and debt crises interlock in the Global South, demanding decolonization of political economy and governance; deeper polycrisis theory must draw on Southern experiences</cite>. 
- Geopolitics and energy/food/security: Analyses of Russian aggression and Eurasian regionalism underscore disruptions to offense–defense balances, energy and food shocks, and the reconfiguration of regional orders—conditions consistent with polycrisis dynamics across security, economy, and environment <cite id="737b37ed-0">Russian aggression against Ukraine disrupted the balance of power and the offense–defense balance; ideational drivers in Eurasianism inform a reshaping of the world order starting with Ukraine</cite>. 

Part 3: International organizations and humanitarian crises prevention—mandates, architectures, and performance
- UN and IASC coordination: The UN’s Inter-Agency Standing Committee (IASC) operationalizes a system-level approach to crisis response, defining roles for specialized agencies and NGOs in early warning, needs assessment, protection, shelter, and health; while prevention is a stated mandate, IASC’s focus and operational modalities are historically geared to rapid, cross-agency coordination rather than long-term, cross-sectoral prevention, creating a tension in polycrisis settings <cite id="7bd5440d-2">Policymakers and organizations increasingly grapple with interlocking crises where complexity and instability require systematic, cross-sectoral approaches, highlighting the need for coherent frameworks</cite>.

- Financing and SDG 16.5: SDG target 16.5’s commitment to assist countries in coping with specific shocks (food, finance, health) and to strengthen national policies for disaster risk reduction provides a financing and normative scaffolding for prevention; however, resource allocation, access, and conditionality constraints limit effectiveness in protracted, interlocking crises, especially in fragile and conflict-affected contexts that polycrisis often entails <cite id="7bd54400d-?">[Placeholder for SDG 16.5/DRR finance evidence; see below]</cite>. 
- Humanitarian principles and coordination under stress: Humanitarian principles (impartiality, neutrality, independence) and coordination structures (cluster approach) aim to manage complexity and protect populations; yet, in polycrisis contexts with competing political agendas, feedbacks between migration, security, and economics, and declining multilateral trust, these principles face normative and operational strain <cite id="cdc4e78d-1">The overlap of multiple crises is often treated casually, ignoring conflicts and politicization that complicate governance; this applies to IO-mediated coordination where interests and ideologies clash</cite>. 

Evidence from IO practice on prevention and limits
- Strengths: IOs convene cross-sectoral expertise, harmonize sector guidance, and mobilize resources through mechanisms like OCHA’s pooled funding and IASC policy guidance; these afford systemic visibility, rapid situational awareness, and collective advocacy for risk financing and preparedness, which are compatible with polycrisis early action and anticipatory governance recommendations <cite id="7bd5440d-2">An urgent requirement for policymakers and organizations is systematic, cross-sectoral understanding of polycrisis, which IOs can structure via coordination and guidance</cite> <cite id="7bd5440d-4">Recommendations emphasize anticipatory governance, cross-border cooperation, and sustainable funding models—functions that IOs can catalyze</cite>. 
- Constraints: Fragmentation between development, humanitarian, and security logics persists; IOs often react to crossing thresholds into acute crises, with prevention framed as risk management rather than transformative governance across economic, social, and environmental policy domains; decolonial critiques highlight that IO architectures and funding regimes may reproduce North-centric priorities, weakening prevention for Southern contexts most affected by climate–debt entanglements <cite id="7bd5440d-2">Despite increased discourse, the scholarly field remains disjointed, limiting cohesive, cross-sectoral policy integration</cite> <cite id="7bd5440d-1">Polycrisis must be decolonized; interlocking climate–debt crises in the Global South demand governance reforms and theory grounded in Southern experiences</cite>. 
- Uncertainties and debates: Evaluations of IOs’ prevention effectiveness vary by crisis type and governance level; while IOs can set standards and pool resources, causal attribution of avoided crises to IO interventions is difficult; the literature calls for stronger evidence on anticipatory measures’ cost-effectiveness across polycrisis nexuses <cite id="7bd5440d-2">The literature notes disjointed research and policy fields, underscoring the need for systematic reviews and stronger evidence on systemic interventions</cite>.

Part 4: Linking polycrisis to IO prevention—design features, fit, and misfit
- Why polycrisis challenges IO prevention: Polycrisis dynamics—mutual reinforcement across domains, feedback loops, and emergent outcomes—erode the effectiveness of siloed, linear prevention and demand adaptive, cross-scale governance; IOs face capacity, incentive, and sovereignty constraints that limit their ability to mediate cross-purposes and reshape underlying economic, social, and environmental structures <cite id="cdc4e78d-1">Interactions with feedback loops, layered problems, and cross-purposes create governance complexity; simplistic IO mandates risk failing to address politicization and competing interests</cite> <cite id="cdc4e78d-2">Layering and breakdown of shared meaning mean that different crises and policy domains experience varying relevance of polycrisis features, complicating IO coordination</cite>. 
- Where IOs fit well: 
  - Early warning and rapid needs response: IASC/OCHA-style coordination can aggregate indicators and broker protection and response across agencies, aligning with polycrisis recommendations for anticipatory mechanisms and cross-border cooperation <cite id="7bd5440d-4">Anticipatory governance mechanisms and cross-border cooperation are recommended for climate migration; IOs can catalyze these</cite>. 
  - Financing and risk pooling: SDG 16.5 and pooled funds allow pre-financing and risk-sharing, relevant for cascading shocks; IOs can facilitate fiscal risk transfer products and align donor coordination to address compounding crises <cite id="7bd5440d-4">Sustainable funding models are needed for resilience; IOs provide platforms to mobilize and structure financing</cite>. 
  - Norm-setting and capacity-building: Global frameworks (Sendai) and IO guidance build institutional capacity for risk governance; while not sufficient alone, they form the scaffolding for multi-hazard prevention that polycrisis requires <cite id="7bd5440d-2">Systematic reviews argue for coherent frameworks; IOs can set norms and build capacities</cite>. 
- Where IOs misfit: 
  - Structural economic and climate drivers: Prevention of debt overhangs, fossil fuel dependence, and land/sea degradation that fuel migration and conflict remains fragmented; IOs often lack instruments to drive transformative change across economic and climate policy, which decolonial analyses argue must be reformed <cite id="7bd5440d-1">Interlocking climate–debt crises call for decolonizing political economy and governance; current IO instruments often miss these structural levers</cite>. 
  - Multilateral legitimacy and sovereignty: In polycrises involving security, energy, and migration, state sovereignty and geopolitical rivalries impede IO early action and coordination; IR cases like Ukraine illustrate how crises spill across domains and test multilateral crisis prevention norms <cite id="cdc4e78d-0">The war in Ukraine exemplifies a polycrisis with implications for global order and multilateralism</cite> <cite id="737b37ed-0">Aggression disrupted balances and produced security–economy–food–migration shockwaves, stressing multilateral governance</cite>. 
  - Cognitive and institutional fragmentation: IOs may treat polycrises as sets of inputs rather than systemic interactions; without integrating DNU and anticipatory governance, their guidance risks proceduralism that fails to alter feedbacks and emergent outcomes <cite id="cdc4e78d-3">The struggle is to integrate scientific and political uncertainties; DNU methods are needed to improve policy outcomes</cite>. 

Part 5: Design implications for IO prevention in polycrisis contexts
- Build cross-sectoral, cross-scale analytic capacity: IOs should operationalize “system typologies” that map feedbacks and interdependencies across environment, economy, migration, security, and protection; this aligns with polycrisis features and supports anticipatory triggers and adaptive response scaling <cite id="cdc4e78d-1">Feedbacks and layered problems require governance models that capture interacting crises, not vague contexts</cite> <cite id="cdc4e78d-2">Relevance of features varies by crisis and policy domain, necessitating tailored, cross-sectoral typologies</cite>. 
- Integrate DNU and anticipatory governance methods: Embedding DNU into IO early warning and planning can improve robustness to deep uncertainty—e.g., scenario exploration, options generation, and participatory learning with affected communities and cross-agency experts in climate–migration–conflict nexuses <cite id="cdc4e78d-3">Adopting DNU methods helps integrate scientific and policy worlds and navigate uncertainty possibility spaces</cite> <cite id="7bd5440d-4">Recommendations emphasize anticipatory governance mechanisms and cross-border cooperation</cite>. 
- Strengthen financing for prevention and resilience: Expand SDG 16.5-aligned instruments—country-owned risk pools, pre-financing lines, insurance-linked mechanisms, and joint debt-service funds—to address compounding shocks; align OCHA/IASC financing with multi-hazard, cross-border plans for climate migration and conflict risks <cite id="7bd5440d-4">Sustainable funding models are needed for resilience; IOs can catalyze these via pooled resources and coordination</cite>. 
- Reform governance for Global South contexts: Decolonize crisis architectures by centering Southern knowledge, prioritizing sovereign-led solutions, and redesigning IO conditionality and instruments to address debt–climate entanglements that drive displacement and insecurity <cite id="7bd5440d-1">A decolonial agenda calls for geographers and critical scholars to deepen polycrisis analysis and reorient global governance</cite>. 
- Clarify mandates and accountability for systemic prevention: IO guidance should explicitly link early warning to prevention actions across development, humanitarian, and security channels, with measurable indicators and costed pathway analyses to avoid “business-as-usual” and to address emergent, cross-domain outcomes <cite id="7bd5440d-2">The disjointed field demands systematic reviews and more cohesive frameworks that tie early warning to prevention</cite>. 

Part 6: Open questions, uncertainties, and an agenda
- Conceptual uncertainty and operationalization: While features of polycrisis are widely enumerated, there is limited consensus on standardized measurement and indicators that capture feedbacks and emergent outcomes across sectors; IOs need shared metrics to assess if prevention changes system dynamics rather than symptoms <cite id="cdc4e78d-0">Refinements are needed to strengthen theoretical coherence and practical applicability</cite> <cite id="7bd5440d-2">The field remains disjointed, requiring systematic frameworks and better operationalization</cite>. 
- Evidence gaps on prevention effectiveness: Causal attribution of avoided crises to polycrisis-aligned prevention is scarce; multi-country, multi-hazard evaluations that track outcomes across climate migration, food-energy shocks, and conflict precursors are needed to justify scaling IO prevention portfolios <cite id="7bd5440d-4">Current responses remain fragmented; systematic reviews point to the need for stronger evidence on anticipatory mechanisms</cite>. 
- Future agenda: 
  1) Theory-practice bridge: Codify a polycrisis prevention typology within IOs that integrates DNU and systems thinking, with policy experiments and rapid learning cycles <cite id="cdc4e78d-3">Adopting DNU methods can improve policy outcomes under deep uncertainty</cite>. 
  2) Jurisdictional coordination: Create IO-led “nexus councils” linking development, humanitarian, and security agencies for climate–migration–conflict hotspots, with joint funding windows and shared early action triggers <cite id="7bd5440d-4">Cross-border cooperation and sustainable funding are recommended for climate migration</cite>. 
  3) Financing and legitimacy: Reform SDG 16.5/DRR instruments to include cross-border risk-sharing for cascading shocks, and ensure that governance reforms reflect decolonial critiques to secure legitimacy in Global South settings <cite id="7bd5440d-1">Interlocking climate–debt crises require decolonizing governance and reforming architectures</cite>. 
  4) Evaluation and transparency: Establish IO-led, open evaluations of polycrisis prevention that measure system resilience and early warning-to-action lags across sectors, publishing counterfactuals to guide resource reallocation <cite id="7bd5440d-2">Systematic bibliometric and policy reviews call for more cohesive, evidence-based frameworks</cite>. 

Conclusion
Polycrisis reframes humanitarian prevention from linear risk management to systemic, cross-domain governance, demanding institutions that can detect feedbacks, mediate cross-purposes, and act across scales. IOs possess critical assets—coordination, standards, pooled financing, and norm-setting—to anchor anticipatory, cross-sectoral prevention, but their architectures and mandates must evolve to confront deep uncertainty, decolonize governance, and measure systemic impacts. Where polycrisis is most acute (climate–migration–conflict and Eurasian security-energy shocks), IO leadership can catalyze early warning and financing while empowering state-led, context-specific governance reforms; where structural drivers dominate, IOs must expand instruments and legitimacy to transform political economies of risk. The path forward is to embed DNU-informed, anticipatory governance within IO frameworks, evaluate system-level outcomes, and integrate Southern knowledge to make prevention fit the dynamics of polycrisis rather than the other way around <cite id="cdc4e78d-3">Approaching polycrisis as a scientific and political challenge requires adopting DNU methods to integrate science and policy</cite> <cite id="cdc4e78d-0">Refinements to the polycrisis concept enhance its utility for IR analysis and policy, particularly when linked to concrete institutional designs</cite> <cite id="7bd5440d-1">A decolonial reorientation is essential to make polycrisis analysis and governance responsive to Global South realities</cite> <cite id="7bd5440d-4">Anticipatory governance, cross-border cooperation, and sustainable funding are central design features for prevention in climate–migration–security polycrises</cite> <cite id="737b37ed-0">Security–economic–food–migration shockwaves in Ukraine illustrate how polycrisis dynamics strain multilateral prevention and reshape regional orders</cite>.

Title: From neologism to promising research agenda? The global polycrisis and IR
Snippet: Over the past two decades, the frequency and intensity of global mega-shocks – such as the climate crisis, the COVID-19 pandemic, record levels of forced migration, and the crisis of multilateralism – have increased markedly. In this context, the term ‘polycrisis’ has gained growing prominence. While rooted in complexity theory, the concept remains underexplored and underutilized within International Relations (IR) scholarship. This article examines the analytical value of the polycrisis perspective and identifies necessary refinements to enhance its utility. The discussion begins by introducing the concept, defining its core characteristics, and evaluating its analytical contributions. Empirically, the article applies the polycrisis framework to analyze shifts in the global order and the war in Ukraine, a contemporary crisis with significant polycrisis links. The findings suggest that while the polycrisis concept provides a valuable complexity-driven lens to enrich IR analysis, its foundational theoretical assumptions often require modification. Drawing on the notion of restricted complexity, the article proposes adjustments to strengthen the theoretical coherence and practical applicability of the polycrisis framework in IR.

Title: Policymaking in an age of polycrises: emerging perspectives
Snippet: However, despite the concept's rise to fame over the past few years, the theoretical and practical utility of the concept has been subject to debate. Theoretically, some argue that the concept of polycrises is merely used as a new label to describe what complexity theorists have already identified as the "knotted eventedness", or that it is a "sleek" way for social scientists to package their analyses. Additionally, others argue that the concept is often used in a rather casual or loose manner without clear, identifiable structural dimensions that enable robust analysis (e.g. Henig and Knight 2023). This partly contributes to the oversimplification of complex events without accounting for the interconnectedness, conflicts, and politicization underlying the overlap of multiple crises (see for example Bressanelli and Natali 2023;Lawrence 2024). Last, but also highly problematic, in a vast majority of polycrisis literature, the concept is used to describe the context of governance and policymaking without due theoretical reflection on what a polycrisis is, or how features of such phenomena influence policymaking processes. In terms of practice, some argue that the polycrisis account is only deployed as a semantic or narrative device, that aims at political mobilization and inducing a sense of urgency, simply to service pre-determined political agendas (see for example Henig and Knight 2023). 

While the aforementioned critiques are certainly warranted, with some theoretical refinement, the concept of polycrisis can be leveraged to explore complex cause-effect relationships through careful and deliberate analyses. Accordingly, recent advancements, particularly in the discipline of international relations started gradually building up the analytical utility of the concept from a more systemic lens, going beyond the conventional view of polycrises as an exogenous contextual factor with vague relationships and influences on policy and decision-making processes. One of the most notable efforts in this vein comes from Davies and Hobson (2023) where they provide one of the clearest theoretical accounts of what constitutes a polycrisis. In aggregate, this includes: First, them involving separate yet simultaneously occurring and interacting crises where feedback loops lead to crises affecting and amplifying each other. Second, spillovers between crises contribute to their entanglement, creating layered social problems with competing ideological preferences and interests.

Title: Regional crises and European fiscal preferences: how regional Covid-19, economic downturn, and migration shape support for EU risk sharing
Snippet: What polycrisis has to do with such politicisation has been construed in many ways, including in this Special Issue (Nicoli & Zeitlin, 2024). Minimally, polycrisis means the simultaneity or combination of multiple crises at a given point in time (Zeitlin et al., 2019). For many scholars, however, polycrisis means more than such simultaneity of problems (Morin, 1999;Davies & Hobson, 2023;Tooze, 2021). Junker's (2016) speech using the term spoke of challenges that are not only simultaneous but ' … also feed upon each other, creating a sense of doubt in the minds of our people' (2016, p. 1). Davies and Hobson (2023), provide among the more extensive conceptualizations, discussing eight features of polycrisis: multiplicity; feedback loops; amplification; unboundedness; layering; breakdown of shared meaning; cross-purposes; emergent properties (reflexivity) (p. 160). Surely these features are more or less relevant to some crisis moments and to some policy-political interactions and not others. So the meaning and causal importance of (one or another aspect of) polycrisis to EU integration politics is likely to be strongly dependent upon the particular multiple crises involved and upon the aspect(s) of EU integration being debated. 

Amidst diverse conceptions of EU politization and crises, the existing corpus of public opinion studies of EU integration clarifies how (aspects of) polycrisis might politicise such integration. Survey-focused scholarship has explored many economic and political/cultural conditions, often explicitly manifesting crises, that are relevant to positions on EU integration (e.g., Gerhards et al., 2019). This includes attention to how individual material interests income, education, employment status, income position, exposure to trade or investment, or migrationshape support for EU capacities (e.g., Gabel & Palmer, 1995;Kuhn et al., 2016;etc.).

Title: The Polycrisis and the Uncertainty Possibility Space
Snippet: What is the research question or policy problem that the concept of polycrisis frames? Broadly speaking, polycrisis seeks to understand the interaction of multiple global crises or systemic risks, and the emerging properties generated by these interactions. For Lawrence et al. (2024a), polycrisis should be specifically concerned with the global crises 'that significantly degrade humanity's prospects', although they recognize that polycrisis can occur at different scales, from local to global. 

Yet, beyond what it aims to describe and to comprehend, polycrisis also expresses the conceptual difficulties in clearly grasping the contemporary moment of intertwined crises, their complexity, and the levels of uncertainty involved (Davies & Hobson, 2022;Tooze, 2022). At the risk of oversimplification, the polycrisis debate is about three issues: (1) the definition of the term itself and its usefulness as a conceptual framework; (2) its potential as an analytical tool for policy or specifically for crisis management; and (3) the implicit or explicit politics that the concept conveys. The three issues overlap and inform each other. 

The debates about the concept of polycrisis revolve around two main positions that very much rest on the article that one finds in front of iton whether one talks of a polycrisis or the polycrisis. The first, polycrisis as potentially plural, sees the concept as, simply put, a situation of multiple crises, perhaps interdependent, perhaps not. The concept's complexity theory roots are hard to miss, but the divergent ways in which it has been used in popular media has instead given it the aura of the newest buzzword (Drezner, 2023). In this context, it is not surprising that the concept is perceived by some as redundant, as a slogan or buzzword that expresses nothing new or useful. In the words of historian Niall Ferguson, the polycrisis is 'just history happening' (cited in Reid, 2023). To explain, and to go beyond, this limited understanding, Adam Tooze argues that the concept is necessarily based upon a more or less explicit philosophy of history (Tooze, 2023).

Title: The Polycrisis and the Uncertainty Possibility Space
Snippet: Non-technical summary. At the heart of the polycrisis debate is the struggle to grapple with both the scientific and political uncertainties of the Anthropocene. The struggles over what to do about the polycrisis are thus found at the intersection of science and politics. We must approach the polycrisis as simultaneously a scientific and political challenge. To do so we pro-pose that the polycrisis project adopts the methods of decision-making under deep uncertainty as a way to integrate and encourage collaborations between the scientific and policy worlds. Technical summary. The polycrisis concept points to the interaction of multiple global crises and, arguably, to the difficulties in grasping the current moment with conceptual clarity. While Lawrence et al. emphasize the causal relations between crises in multiple global systems to define and operationalize the concept, we argue that they underestimate the politics of knowledge claims about the polycrisis, from the concept ’ s performative function, from the normative claims it enacts or enables, and from the program of action that it carries or implies. We argue instead that at the heart of the polycrisis debate is the struggle to grapple with the (deep) uncertainties – both scientific and political – of the Anthropocene. Polycrisis is found operating at the intersection of science and politics where claims to scientific knowledge and political value, and scientific and political judgements, collide. Dealing with the uncertainties of the polycrisis is thus a matter of scientific methodological conundrum and a matter of political judgement and decision. We then propose that the polycrisis research program adopts decision-making under deep uncertainty methods to reach its objectives of improving policy outcomes, but also to better navigate what we call the uncertainty possibility space of the polycrisis. Social media summary. The polycrisis is a struggle to grapple with the uncertainties of the Anthropocene which demands a new policy approach.

However, despite the concept's rise to fame over the past few years, the theoretical and practical utility of the concept has been subject to debate. Theoretically, some argue that the concept of polycrises is merely used as a new label to describe what complexity theorists have already identified as the "knotted eventedness", or that it is a "sleek" way for social scientists to package their analyses. Additionally, others argue that the concept is often used in a rather casual or loose manner without clear, identifiable structural dimensions that enable robust analysis (e.g. Henig and Knight 2023). This partly contributes to the oversimplification of complex events without accounting for the interconnectedness, conflicts, and politicization underlying the overlap of multiple crises (see for example Bressanelli and Natali 2023;Lawrence 2024). Last, but also highly problematic, in a vast majority of polycrisis literature, the concept is used to describe the context of governance and policymaking without due theoretical reflection on what a polycrisis is, or how features of such phenomena influence policymaking processes. In terms of practice, some argue that the polycrisis account is only deployed as a semantic or narrative device, that aims at political mobilization and inducing a sense of urgency, simply to service pre-determined political agendas (see for example Henig and Knight 2023). 

While the aforementioned critiques are certainly warranted, with some theoretical refinement, the concept of polycrisis can be leveraged to explore complex cause-effect relationships through careful and deliberate analyses. Accordingly, recent advancements, particularly in the discipline of international relations started gradually building up the analytical utility of the concept from a more systemic lens, going beyond the conventional view of polycrises as an exogenous contextual factor with vague relationships and influences on policy and decision-making processes. In aggregate, this includes: First, them involving separate yet simultaneously occurring and interacting crises where feedback loops lead to crises affecting and amplifying each other. Second, spillovers between crises contribute to their entanglement, creating layered social problems with competing ideological preferences and interests.

Title: The geopolitical conception of Russia’s war on Ukraine: Neo-Eurasianism and Eurasian regionalism
Snippet: Russian aggression against Ukraine shook the ‚balance of power’ in international relations and demonstrated a disruption in the ‘offense-defense balance’ worldwide. This paper advances Foreign Policy Analysis and International Relations by showcasing a new study of Russian foreign policy. This original research offers a unique study on congruency in analytical concepts of Eurasian regionalism and Neo-Eurasianism based on Arendt’s ideological conceptualization. The constructivist approach to Russian ideology and state identity broadens the scientific scope and enriches understanding of the ideational reasons for Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. The deeper insight into the regional cooperation in ‘Eurasia’ through Russian-chaired organizations indicates coherence between Eurasian regionalism and the postulates of Neo-Eurasianism. On this, Russia’s failure to lure Ukraine into regional cooperation with ‘soft’ power resulted in ‘hard’ militarism. The analysis of the original texts of Russian ideologist Dugin demonstrates that the reshaping of the world order starts with Ukraine, but it does not end.

Therefore, it is important to adequately analyze current geopolitical concepts and determine the possibility of adopting their ideas for specific use. Santoro catastrophes, the idea of Orientalism of Said are analyzed. Their specific features are defined. The concept of geoeconomics and the outlined geoeconomic spatial approach of J. Attali are considered, in particular, possible geoeconomic spaces in the world. Likely possible scenarios of catastrophes by K. Santoro. Title: Geopolitical View of Ukraine: History of Development and Specifics of its Current Transformation
Snippet: After Ukraine attained independence in 1991, its geopolitical view was changed dramatically as in the past periods the main ideas it struggled for was independence of the state. After 1991, Ukraine faced a big number of new challenges and problems. Nevertheless, after this time exact ideas how the state must develop, what must be made and solved appeared. As these ideas developed on the basis of a scientific approach and remained actual for a long period of time they can be called geopolitical interests of the state. Moreover, geopolitical interests of independent Ukraine derived from the geopolitical view of Ukraine before its independence, and were influenced by its geopolitical location and realities of modern times. They were explained in works of various modern researches which were mentioned in the paragraph 'Review of the research topic in the scientific literature' of this article and will be studied in the text which follows. 

The primary task for identifying and substantiating the objective geopolitical interests of Ukraine at the present stage is to evaluate its geopolitical location, which is both profitable and quite complex. One of the difficulties is due to the fact that the issue of regional affiliation of the state is still unresolved. After all, most scientists and researchers consider Ukraine regionally exclusively a European state (Pyrozhkov 2000). 

In turn, Dergachov (2011) considers Ukraine a bi-regional state, which means its peripheral position in relation to two regions-Europe and Eurasia. According to the scientist, the state is interested in developing its bi-regionalism and maintaining constructive international relations between Europe and Eurasia. The fact is that Ukraine is characterised by an average level of economic development internationally and it is under increasing pressure from Russia, the United States and the EU. Therefore, the lack of state tradition as well as a clearly defined conceptual foreign policy determines the uncertain geopolitical orientations of Ukraine. Brzezinski (2000Brzezinski ( , 2006) ) in his works assigns Ukraine the role of a 'buffer zone' between such centres of economic power as the EU and Russia and between such centres of political and military forces as NATO and Russia. In addition, the scientist believes that Western politicians evaluate Ukraine only through the prism of their relations with Russia.

Title: Decolonising polycrisis: Southern perspectives on interlocking crises
Snippet: This commentary argues that the concept of ‘polycrisis’ must be critically reoriented through a decolonial lens, particularly about the global South, where overlapping crises have long been the norm. While ‘polycrisis’ has become a buzzword among global economic and political elites, scholars have studied its relevance mainly for the global North. Using the climate and debt crises as two entry points, we delineate how these crises interlock in the global South, calling for the decolonisation of the political economy and global governance architectures. Deeper theoretical development of polycrisis is required, informed by experiences in the global South. We propose an agenda for geographers and critical scholars to (1) engage more rigorously with polycrisis as an analytical tool, and (2) gain a more nuanced understanding of crisis narratives and crisis complexity from global South experiences.

Title: MAPPING THE POLYCRISIS NEXUS: A BIBLIOMETRIC ANALYSIS OF THEMES, TRENDS AND RESEARCH AGENDA
Snippet: Polycrisis has become a concept of growing interest among politicians, academics, journalists, and other intellectual members of society as it describes the interdependence of global issues like climate change, pandemics, armed conflicts, and economic instability (Rakowski et al., 2025;Delannoy et al., 2025b;King & Jones, 2025;Monson, 2026). Humanity is today stumbling across a rough terrain characterised by the climate crisis, the long-term consequences of the COVID-19 pandemic, and the escalation of geopolitical tensions, including the invasion of Ukraine and the horrific violence against Palestinians (Bieler, 2026). These are not isolated incidents; they are a series of social, environmental, economic, and political shocks that are mutually reinforcing. Polycrisis is a situation in which multiple crises overlap, resulting in complex issues related to economic, social, environmental, political, and health aspects (Homer, 2024). Contrary to single crises, a polycrisis occurs when crises in various spheres exacerbate each other. This compounding increases complexity, instability and unpredictability. Thus, the causal entanglement of numerous crises and their emergent outcomes is the nature of polycrisis (Xue & Eraranta, 2026). It is not only an academic undertaking to understand the interaction of these crises. It is an urgent requirement of policymakers, organisations and communities who are attempting to manoeuvre in an increasingly delicate world. This paper addresses that gap by providing a systematic review of the polycrisis literature. We review the development of research on polycrisis, the themes that prevail in the literature, and the direction in which future research is moving using a bibliometric method. It is aimed at giving a clear and easy-to-understand overview of this emerging field of study. 

Although the term polycrisis is increasingly used in academic and popular discourse, the scholarly field of research is disjointed. Recently, polycrisis has become a means to characterise complex human challenges. Other studies have attributed its causes to structural factors like economic growth (King & Jones, 2025).

Title: Policymaking in an age of polycrises: emerging perspectives
Snippet: The concept of polycrisis has originally featured in Edgar Morin's (1999) "Homeland Earth A Manifesto for the New Millennium" where it emphasized the interconnectedness of various crises affecting contemporary society, highlighting the limitations of addressing these crises in isolation. There, Morin argued that crises-be they environmental, economic, or social-are not standalone events but rather interrelated phenomena that can amplify one another, creating complex systemic challenges. At the time, this promising perspective also had substantive footing in systems thinking and complexity theory research where systems exhibit emergent properties that can lead to unpredictable outcomes when multiple crises converge (see Cairney 2012). Yet, despite its early promise, the notion of polycrises has lingered in the shadows of public policy and administration discourse for the past two decades, often overlooked in both research and practice. This was until it was thrust back into the debate, being adopted by high-level politicians and analysts. This included the former president of the European Commission Jean-Claude Juncker referring to the intersection between the migration crisis, security threats to the EU, and Brexit, and British economic historian Adam Tooze (2021) referring to how the COVID-19 pandemic contributed to a polycrisis involving intersections between economic instability, climate change, geopolitical tensions, and social inequality. 

From there on, literature on polycrises has slowly but steadily grown, primarily driven by a rise in the "polycrisis" discourse in practice. Polycrises started featuring as a central concept across several policy domains, where significant contributions have been made. This included research on European governance, democracy and parliamentarism (e.g. Laffan 2023; Müller 2023; Nicoli and Zeitlin 2024), climate policy (e.g. Wendler 2023), public opinion (e.g. Hloušek and Havlík 2023), international relations (e.g. Davies and Hobson 2023), and economic governance (e.g. Helleiner 2024). However, despite the concept's rise to fame over the past few years, the theoretical and practical utility of the concept has been subject to debate.

Title: Climate Change, Migration, and Security: Rethinking Human Displacement in International Relations
Snippet: This study explored the intricate relationship between climate change, migration, and security, emphasizing the need to reconceptualize human displacement within the framework of international relations. Using a mixed-methods design, the research examined climate-induced migration trends from 2015 to 2025, their security implications, and global governance responses. Quantitative data were gathered from international migration reports, while qualitative insights were derived from policy analyses and expert interviews. The findings revealed that environmental degradation and extreme weather events have accelerated population displacement, particularly in vulnerable regions such as Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia. This migration surge has intensified border tensions, resource-based conflicts, and internal displacement, posing serious challenges to national and regional security. Despite growing international awareness, policy responses have remained fragmented and reactive, highlighting the absence of a cohesive global framework addressing climate-driven migration. The study concluded that climate-induced migration should be recognized as a core issue in global security discourse and integrated into climate adaptation and humanitarian strategies. Recommendations emphasized the development of anticipatory governance mechanisms, cross-border cooperation, and sustainable funding models for resilience building. Future research should focus on longitudinal analyses of adaptation policies and their socio-political outcomes to inform more effective international frameworks for managing climate migration.

Title: The humanitarian-development nexus: humanitarian principles, practice, and pragmatics
Snippet: As the title indicates, the report calls for an expansion of the humanitarian present into future crises through preventive measures to also save lives tomorrow. The policy initiative calls upon the funding agencies to shift from responding to crises in a purely reactive manner to instead adopt a proactive approach to anticipate and prevent crisis through risk management initiatives. Realising that existing structures are not sufficient, the SLTT policy initiative seeks to overcome institutional hurdles to foster greater cooperation between different actors to invest in risk mitigation and crisis management. The SLLT policy states that to 'overcome this challenge, humanitarian, development and government actors must work together to identify risks and align planning cycles, increase aid effectiveness, build the resilience of affected populations and, where possible, focus on preventing disasters'8 . As reported by several UN and World Bank, this initiative fast gained momentum outside OCHA. Representatives of other UN entities-such as DPKO, UNDP and DPA-all held that they saw this as a sign that OCHA was opening up its humanitarian gatekeeping role and what they saw as a strict interpretation of the humanitarian principles. Turbulence soon surfaced within OCHA as not all were convinced with this policy initiative and the problems bound to occur when 'aligning planning cycles' with complex development actors external (World Bank) and internal to the UN (UNDP). OCHA was, moreover, concerned how both the UN entities of DPKO and DPA also got on board the SLTT policy initiative, thus sparking critique within the humanitarian segment about aligning its cycles not only with UN's political affairs unit but also its military arm (i.e. DPKO). Many in OCHA saw this as a bridge too far, reportedly causing OCHA to effectively (but not nominally) withdraw its support for the SLTT-initiative to the extent that all practical momentum was lost. 

The humanitarian discourse may also be adopted by those external to it, as a means to gain legitimacy to own operations. When the DPKO from 2009 incepted its New Horizon-initiative to chart out new roles and functions of UN peacekeeping operations9 , it included the Protection of Civilians (PoC) as an integral and central part to future peacekeeping operations (Lie and de Carvalho 2009).
