Title: Multilateral Humanitarian Aid As a Foreign Socio-Humanitarian Policy Tool in Britain
Snippet: The article proposes to single out socio-humanitarian cooperation as a separate foreign policy tool. It studies the case of the UK to demonstrate the synergy between conceptual approaches and their implementation in the national legislation in providing official development assistance (ODA) and humanitarian aid as the two integral parts of socio-humanitarian policy. The authors conclude that the shift in doctrinal priorities in the area, including the prioritisation of emergency aid and individual recipients (Afghanistan, certain African states) after 2020, is confirmed by the change in London's approaches towards UN humanitarian agencies, with the pace of cuts to humanitarian aid funds being faster than the government's stated targets. Based on statistical data from 2005‒2023, the authors distinguish two periods of the UK's multilateral socio-humanitarian policy: 2005‒2020 and 2020 ‒ to the present. The first period saw the growth in London's emergency response funding being in line with the overall growth in global humanitarian needs. In the second period, despite the dramatic increase in the funds requested by UN agencies and the general degradation of the global humanitarian situation (the humanitarian appeal of the UN's main coordination mechanism, the Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), increased from $39 bn in 2020 to $51.5 bn in 2023, with the number of people in dire need jumping from 98 million in 2020 to 230 million in 2023), UK deprioritised practically all channels of multilateral humanitarian funding. For the second period, we show the emphasis on food aid, along with a staggering (up to 85%) reduction in other funding areas, most notably in unearmarked contributions and CERF pledges. Such a change may be explained, on the one hand, by the deteriorating food security situation in key recipient countries and, on the other hand, by the politicisation of humanitarian assistance on the part of the UK.

Title: Nuancing the double and triple nexus: analyzing the potential for unintended, negative consequences
Snippet: Humanitarian, development, and peace actions are often funded and implemented in distinct ways, within unique operational paradigms, and by different actors. However, certain contexts require humanitarian, development, and peace actions in parallel, either geographically or temporally. Additionally, many circumstances require flexibility to shift between programming modalities due to changing contexts. Due to these realities, intergovernmental, governmental, and non-governmental agencies have called for a nexus approach which has had two distinct iterations, the humanitarian-development nexus and the humanitarian-development-peace nexus, the former emerging in literature and practice prior to the latter (ICVA 2017;OCHA n.d.;UNDP n.d.). For ease of readability, and as both are studied within this article, we hence forth will be referring to the humanitarian-development nexus as the 'double nexus' and the humanitarian-development-peace nexus as the 'triple nexus'. 

The double and triple nexus are presented by the United Nations (UN) as an approach to assistance that requires broad partnership amongst UN agencies, nongovernmental organizations (NGOs), civil society organizations (CSOs), the private sector, and governments, but also as a need for internal reform (ICVA 2017). The United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) and United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) in particular, have emerged as some of the leading UN agencies in advancing the double and triple nexus agenda which the OCHA describes as an assistance program that is working to achieve collective outcomes (ICVA 2017;OCHA n.d.;UNDP n.d.). According to a statement made by the UN Secretary General, the organization's aim is to enhance collaboration across UN subsidiaries, a goal shared by both the double and triple nexus, while also placing greater emphasis on instability, exclusion, vulnerability, and conflict prevention, marking a distinct shift towards the dominance of the triple nexus in the international sphere (ECOSOC 2017). 

The UN and its subsidiaries draw on the 2030 Agenda and Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) as their justification of the need for a triple nexus approach (ECOSOC 2017).

Title: “Post-Non-Classical” or “Post-Neoclassical” Epistemology?
Snippet: The social and humanitarian sciences are dispersed and fragmented due to their disciplinary boundaries. Consequently, the completeness, integrity, complexity, and multidimensionality of social objects under study are not "addressed" by current cognitive processes [12, p. 21]. 

Philosophers employ figurative language to convey the epistemological, methodological, and psychological implications of contradictions and difficulties in a way that encourages a willingness to "look at the face of complexity without fear" [13]. In this context, contemporary philosophers emphasise other points of epistemological and methodological importance. 

For instance, V. Arshinov and B. Budanov posit that the structures of interdisciplinary understanding within the complexity paradigm are inherently uncertain. Among the various cognitive problems that emerge at this time, the "complexity problem formulation" occupies a distinctive position. It is characterised by a "complex logical" and "non-linear process" [4]. 

In their latest research, V. Arshinov and V. Budanov examine the phenomenon of complexity in the context of the formation of "quantum semiotics." Philosophers posit that a "conceptual character" endowed with the capacity to observe and comprehend complexity should be formed. Such a cognitive observer can be considered a perceiving subject "in the unity of cyber semiotic, synergetic and quantummechanical perspectives" [4, p. 67]. 

In such complexity, it is challenging to demonstrate a single epistemological and methodological position in their context in the philosophical approach to scientific rationality and epistemological features. Indeed, researchers have observed that searching for solutions to the abovementioned difficulties led to postnon-classicism and post-non-classical rationality. This process revealed the existence of multivariate ness. 

In particular, post-non-classicism ideas, as they have been formed in the social and humanitarian sciences, can be divided into three groups. The first group comprises scientific research activities that employ interdisciplinary and polyparadigmatic approaches. This approach selects system analysis (synergistic) as a methodological foundation. System analysis synthesises natural science, social, and humanitarian sciences. In this regard, philosophers have separately observed that V. Stepin established a "universal discourse" for the dialogue between natural science and humanitarian "cultures" [15].
</snippet>

Title: Synthesis, part of a Special Feature on Applied Research for Enhancing Human Well-Being and Environmental Stewardship: Using Complexity Thinking in Southern Africa Exploring the implications of critical complexity for the study of social- ecological systems.
Snippet: Morin (2008:33) critiques the former as a reaction to reductionism, which insists on a kind of holism that is "...never anything more than a plastic bag enveloping whatever it found any way it could, and...the more the totality becomes full, the emptier it becomes." Such holism is a strong form of constructivism that negates the need for a reliable ontology, as reality is described in terms of our knowledge thereof (Preiser 2012). Despite the strong opposition to reductionism inherent in this view, it is precisely such a strategy that is employed in reducing all ontology to epistemology (Preiser 2012). In contrast, those complexity theorists who assert that all complexity can be conceptualized and measured in some way adopt a simplifying approach that does not recognize the intangible nature of many emergent properties, for example, a sense of place of a particular area. From this perspective, emergence is a matter of finding the right rules and laws to define the extent of complexity at hand. The idea that all complexity can be formalized, for example, by expression in fractals and power laws, remains largely unquestioned. 

These conflicting positions reveal the difficulties in resolving the problem of reductionism in unambiguous terms. Indeed, it is arguable that this problem is the central dilemma in the study of complexity. Cilliers (2005b:261) articulates this dilemma as an inescapable "performative tension" within complexity. This performative tension results from the fact that a rigorous understanding of complexity is one that denies both total holism and total reductionism simultaneously; while still acknowledging that any description of a complex system necessarily performs some reduction of reality (Cilliers 2005b). Therefore, we do not consider a complexity perspective as being in opposition to reductionist research strategies, but rather as both transcending and including such strategies. Here, the study of complex phenomena is at best a postreductionist effort that is necessarily a critical position (Preiser 2012). This insight is central to what Preiser and Cilliers (2010) term "critical complexity." Critical complexity follows the logic of reductionism, with a simultaneous awareness of the choices made in reducing the system.
</snippet>

Title: Understanding sexual violence in armed conflict: cutting ourselves with Occam’s razor
Snippet: Global development expert Ben Ramalingam (2013) suggests that simplicity, i.e. reductionist philosophy (Occam's razor), underlies much of the aid world, adding up to 'a system where simplicity is repeatedly, consistently, and damagingly chosen over relevance and appropriateness ' (p. 125). The consequence of this approach is that the issue cannot be effectively addressed (Wieringa 1998), illustrated by '[g]ender [being] treated as a portable tool of analysis and empowerment that can be carried around in the back pockets of both international humanitarian and development staff' instead of a concept that should inform core understanding (Hyndman and de Alwis 2003, p. 212). Simplicity allows humanitarian actors not only relief from the obligation to investigate structural contexts that (re)produce the occurrence of sexual violence in conflict but also exemption from scrutiny in cases where actors are complicit in (re)producing these structural inequalities. 

This necessitates a paradigm shift from conventional simplicity thinking to complexity thinking-a way of looking at world problems where interconnectivities, dynamics, and complexities are recognised rather than avoided (Ramalingam 2013), and thus towards a more realistic understanding of the issue (Ramalingam et al. 2008). If humanitarians would engage with complexity thinking, Ramalingam (2013) argues, 'the right questions would be asked rather than the right solutions provided; and organisational learning would be fearless and tireless, characterised by co-evolving and learning with 'beneficiaries' rather than for them: the international humanitarian system would be 'as open to change on the inside as it was hungry for change outside" (p. 363). This requires (re)linking not only critical research to humanitarian policy (theory) but also theory to practice. That means that researchers have to be willing to fearlessly engage with feminist thinking and give 'gender' back its political and practical potential, by (re)visualising sexuality and the symbolic dimensions of sexual violence in armed conflict (Wieringa 1998).
</snippet>

Title: Humanitarian virtue: identifying ethics and values in humanitarian thinking
Snippet: By disaggregating and rethinking humanitarianisms in an ethical context we seek to assist the metacognitive thinking required to deconstruct and reconstruct humanitarianism in ways that point to what lies behind the actions: the values and judgements inherent in diverse responses to urgent human need. In a way, our categories encompass and extend Peters' (2019, p. 1184) analysis and critique of humanitarian systems, which he argues take three main forms: 'a political critique that links humanitarianism with international politics of the West; an economic critique that examines humanitarianism as a growing global business; and, a critique that focuses on the pervasive "everyday nature" of humanitarianism and its growing professionalization'. Likewise, DuBois' (2018, p. 1) analysis of the humanitarian sector highlights the need for a vision for future humanitarianism that is 'responsive, ethical and attainable', and 'less paternalistic, bureaucratic and expansive in its ambitions'. He proposes a 'scaled-down and rescoped alternative to humanitarianism's dysfunctional exercise in interventionist, international charity' (DuBois, 2018, p. 1). 

We take particular note of DuBois' (2018, p. 1) critique of the 'increasingly prominent mismatch between the needs of people in crisis and the assumptions, approaches and skills of humanitarians' owing to the lack of coherence and inter-disciplinarity in approaches, and we try not to perpetuate this in our own methodology. By contextualising humanitarianisms within ethical thinking from different times, cultures, and value systems, we attempt to make a small contribution to decentring Western, neoliberal, or other hegemonic positions, asking what values are present rather than using any single value set as a criterion for evaluation. 

In this way we both see and seek patterns, and we argue that see(k)ing order in this manner will assist metacognition of humanitarian principles and thinking in the broader context of the twenty-first century and the immense political, economic, and environmental changes we are witnessing. Beyond theory, however, we contend that this has value in the messy spaces of practice, by giving practitioners better tools to understand colleagues, communities, and even competitors.

Summary answer
International organizations’ polycrisis-driven humanitarian prevention literature contains both technocratic management framings and substantive critiques of reductionist intervention paradigms. On the managerial side, IO practice operationalizes complexity through real-time dashboards, quantitative risk models, anticipatory and whole‑of‑society policies, and performance frameworks that render complex risk legible and governable. At the same time, critical humanitarians argue that such formalization often co-opts complexity into managerialism, obscuring structural power and meaning; they advocate “critical complexity” that remains reflexive about reductionism and calls for prevention approaches that ask the right questions rather than only delivering prepackaged solutions. The field thus simultaneously tames complexity via technocratic instruments and contests those instruments as incomplete without deeper political and epistemic reflexivity. <cite id="7f040b94-0">The polycrisis concept is rooted in complexity theory and has been advanced as a promising but underutilized lens that IOs can adapt for practical applicability in security and crisis governance</cite> <cite id="7f040b94-4">Polycrisis scholarship emphasizes that organizations must combine adaptive responses with mechanisms that stabilize core operations and coordinate across public, private, and nongovernmental actors because wicked problems rarely fall within the authority of a single organization</cite>.

How IOs operationalize complexity: technocratic management framings
- Real-time information platforms and decision support: OCHA’s Humanitarian Dashboard consolidates multi‑sector needs and contextual indicators in real time to inform response decisions, signaling a managerial turn that treats complex interdependencies as data streams to be monitored, compared, and acted upon. OCHA paired this with preparedness pilots that emphasize measurable deliverables and performance frameworks at country/region levels, explicitly tying complexity to trackable outputs and managerial accountability. <cite id="9e86776f-0">OCHA developed the Humanitarian Dashboard to consolidate and communicate multi‑sector needs in real time for better decision making, and introduced preparedness pilots with measurable deliverables and performance frameworks at country and regional levels</cite>.
- Quantitative risk modeling and allocation optimization: OCHA’s Global Focus Model (GFM) and the World Bank’s Global Urban Risk Index exemplify a risk-based paradigm that formalizes hazard, vulnerability, capacity and humanitarian focus into optimization models for resource allocation, thereby operationalizing “complexity” as quantifiable inputs to managerial prioritization. <cite id="9e86776f-1">OCHA’s Global Focus Model optimizes aid allocation using hazard, vulnerability, capacity and humanitarian foci, updated annually; the World Bank’s Global Urban Risk Index supports prioritization and transition from managing emergencies to managing risks</cite>.
- Anticipation and whole‑of‑governance agendas: IO-led policy initiatives push beyond crisis response to proactive prevention via risk management, urging alignment of humanitarian, development, and government cycles, collective outcomes, and resilience-building—logics that translate complexity into governable risk categories, financing instruments, and inter-agency coordination structures. <cite id="9e86776f-2">Policy initiatives call for expanding the humanitarian present into future crises through preventive measures grounded in risk management, with UN and World Bank backing that spurred internal debate over aligning planning cycles with complex development actors and UN entities</cite> <cite id="9e86776f-4">The UN and OCHA promote a nexus approach requiring broad partnership and internal reform, aiming to achieve collective outcomes, emphasize instability, exclusion, vulnerability and conflict prevention, and frame collaboration in SDG terms</cite>.
- HR and leadership as levers of complex interventions: OCHA recognized leadership gaps and responded with targeted talent strategies to build capacity for complex coordination, reinforcing a managerialist assumption that complexity can be tamed through skilled leadership and organizational design. <cite id="9e86776f-0">OCHA identified leadership as critical, took steps to deploy experienced leaders and develop a comprehensive HR strategy to attract the right talent and skills for complex response and preparedness</cite>.

Limits and critiques: complexity as critique of reductionist paradigms
- Diagnosing reductionism in aid policy and practice: Prominent critiques argue that Occamist simplicity underpins much of the aid system, substituting portable tools and pre-packaged solutions for contextual analysis, thereby failing to address intractable issues like sexual violence in conflict; the proposed remedy is a paradigm shift to complexity thinking that centers interconnectivity, dynamics, and co‑evolving learning with beneficiaries rather than top‑down delivery. <cite id="55ed503b-2">Simplicity and reductionism underlie much of the aid world, producing system-wide irrelevance; a shift to complexity thinking recognizes interconnectivities and dynamics, encouraging co‑evolving learning with beneficiaries and asking the right questions rather than providing pre-packaged solutions</cite>.
- Critical complexity as a post‑reductionist stance: Complexity theorists articulate a central dilemma—formalization tends to flatten emergent properties and reduce ontology to epistemology—yet rigorous complexity also acknowledges partial reduction as necessarily performative; critical complexity argues for methods that transcend and include reductionism while retaining reflexivity about what is lost in simplification. This positions complexity not as a purely technocratic fix but as a critical lens for prevention that safeguards ethical and political inquiry. <cite id="55ed503b-1">Morin critiques reductionist holism that negates ontology; critical complexity holds that all complexity can be conceptualized and measured only partially, and frames emergence as finding the right rules while recognizing intangible properties; it is a postreductionist and necessarily critical position acknowledging performative tension</cite>.
- Beyond financial resilience: Polycrisis research warns that resilience strategies fixated on financial diversification miss governance, authority, and access constraints in concurrent humanitarian and public health crises; coordination capacity and institutional access become as consequential as resources. This critique targets IO-style resilience architectures that risk depoliticizing structural barriers by rendering them as mere inefficiencies to be optimized. <cite id="7f040b94-4">In concurrent crises, organizations must combine adaptive responses with stabilized core operations and cross‑sector coordination; approaches focusing only on financial adaptation may insufficiently capture governance challenges where coordination, authority and institutional access are decisive</cite>.
- Professionalization and ethics: Meta‑ethical critiques of the humanitarian system highlight the mismatch between crises and increasingly professionalized, bureaucratic interventions, calling for scaled‑down, more ethical, and less paternalistic approaches that decentre hegemonic value sets; this positions complexity as a critique of managerial expansionism and calls for humility about what can be operationalized without erasing local meaning. <cite id="55ed503b-4">Analyses identify Western, neoliberal hegemony in humanitarianism and call for a rescoped alternative that is responsive, ethical, less paternalistic and bureaucratic, addressing the mismatch between needs and approaches through decentring and attention to values</cite>.

Synthesis: a dual movement—managerialization and critical reframing—within polycrisis prevention
- The managerial turn is visible in IO practice: OCHA’s dashboard, risk models, and anticipatory policies translate complexity into monitored indicators, allocation formulas, and coordination protocols, while HR and leadership strategies target capacity to manage complex systems. These instruments stabilize operations, enable early warning loops, and create routines for prevention and preparedness that can scale across polycrisis contexts. <cite id="9e86776f-0">OCHA’s dashboard, financing instruments, leadership strategy, and preparedness pilots operationalize complex humanitarian contexts into measurable, coordinated, and accountable processes</cite> <cite id="9e86776f-1">Risk models and indices formalize hazard, vulnerability, capacity, and humanitarian foci into optimization frameworks for resource allocation</cite> <cite id="9e86776f-2">Anticipatory policies expand prevention via risk management and inter‑actor alignment, reframing prevention as a coordinated, whole‑of‑governance activity</cite>.
- Yet IO-linked scholarship also insists that these managerial translations risk becoming new “technoscientific” shells that obscure structural power and irreducible uncertainties. Critical complexity urges prevention to remain reflexive about reductionism, to protect space for feminist and political analyses, and to design learning processes that are as open to internal change as they are to external shocks. <cite id="55ed503b-2">A shift to complexity thinking avoids reductionist tools that displace structural analysis, promoting co‑evolving learning and political reclamation of concepts like gender</cite> <cite id="55ed503b-1">Critical complexity is both a postreductionist effort that transcends and includes reductionist strategies, maintaining a critical stance about what formalization omits</cite>.
- The polycrisis itself pushes IOs toward governance and coordination as core prevention capacities, not just service delivery. This reorientation aligns with critical arguments that complexity cannot be fully tamed by metrics alone; rather, prevention must navigate authority, legitimacy, and institutional access—capabilities that managerial framings alone may not cultivate. <cite id="7f040b94-4">Polycrisis demands combining adaptive responses with stabilized operations and cross‑sector governance because wicked problems span authority silos</cite> <cite id="55ed503b-4">Ethical critiques call for less bureaucratic and paternalistic humanitarianism, emphasizing values and decentring dominant regimes of practice</cite>.

Practical implications for prevention
- Use managerial tools judiciously as boundary objects: Dashboards and risk models are valuable for early detection and equitable allocation, but should be coupled with participatory learning and power analysis to avoid reproducing structural inequities. <cite id="9e86776f-0">OCHA’s dashboard supports real-time, cross-sector decision-making and preparedness measurement</cite> <cite id="55ed503b-2">Complexity thinking insists on co‑evolving with beneficiaries and asking the right questions rather than only delivering solutions</cite>.
- Build “critical systems” capacity: Invest in governance, coordination, and whole‑of‑society architectures that can address authority gaps and legitimacy constraints, not just risk scores. <cite id="9e86776f-4">The nexus approach emphasizes collective outcomes, partnership, and conflict prevention under SDG framing</cite> <cite id="7f040b94-4">Coordination and authority are as consequential as financial flexibility in concurrent humanitarian and public health crises</cite>.
- Maintain reflexivity against technocratic capture: Embed explicit anti‑reductionist practices—qualitative case studies, feminist and political analysis, and iterative theory–practice linking—into anticipatory frameworks to counteract the flattening effects of formalization. <cite id="55ed503b-2">Techniques that treat complex issues as simple tools can sidestep structural context; complexity thinking restores political and conceptual depth</cite> <cite id="55ed503b-1">Critical complexity articulates the inescapable tension between reduction and holism and insists on methodological reflexivity</cite>.

Title: Assessing the political and institutional determinants of international organizational effectiveness: diplomatic mediation, peacebuilding, and human rights advocacy in the context of Pakistan
Snippet: This study examines how global organizations address global issues and promote peace in today's complex geopolitical context. 

In 2023, humanitarian and peacekeeping missions were the primary means by which international organizations addressed crises and conflicts. International groups increased their humanitarian activities to meet the needs of the affected populations. They assisted with food, shelter, and medical care while addressing the root causes of the crisis (ICRC 2023). Due to geopolitics and globalization, international organizations are increasingly involved in crisis management and conflict avoidance. Title: Nonprofit Resilience in Polycrisis: Evidence from Czech NGOs Responding to the Ukrainian Refugee Crisis
Snippet: With the increasing frequency of crises ranging from local disasters to global pandemics, crisis management has become a central concern for public administration and civil society scholars. The concept of polycrisis captures how crises interact and reinforce one another, blurring the boundary between emergency response and routine governance (Morin and Kern 1999;Whiting and Park 2023). Related scholarship on prolonged crises emphasizes that organizations must combine adaptive responses with mechanisms that stabilize core operations as crisis management becomes embedded in everyday governance (Nolte and Lindenmeier 2024). Complex crises also require coordination across public, private, and nongovernmental actors, as wicked problems rarely fall within the authority of a single organization or sector (Ansell and Gash 2008;Denford et al. 2022). Under these conditions, governments increasingly depend on nonprofit organizations and civil society actors to sustain frontline response and fill gaps in state capacity. 

Polycrisis scholarship highlights how crises overlap and accumulate, creating sustained turbulence rather than temporary disruption. A significant portion of the nonprofit resilience literature has focused on financial adaptation and resource diversification (Witmer and Mellinger 2016;Chen 2021;Searing et al. 2023). While valuable, these approaches may insufficiently capture the governance challenges posed by concurrent humanitarian and public health crises, where coordination, authority, and institutional access become as consequential as financial flexibility (Denford et al. 2022;Janssen and van der Voort 2020). This gap points to the need to examine nonprofit resilience in polycrisis conditions where governments shift greater responsibility onto nonprofits without reinforcing the governance and funding structures that sustain them. 

Emerging scholarship on Extreme Context Research (ECR) further clarifies the temporal dynamics of crisis response. ECR shows how organizational strategies evolve across the stages of extreme events, shifting from improvisation in the acute phase toward more routinized coordination as conditions stabilize (Hällgren et al. 2018;Hadida et al. 2015;Hannah et al. 2009). Research on community-based responses during COVID-19 similarly demonstrates how organizations move from emergency mobilization and service provision toward longer-term coordination and recovery activities (Cheng et al. 2020).

Title: Information Management in Disaster and Humanitarian Response: A Case in United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs
Snippet: As discussed in previous sections, during 2010 EGS/OCHA identified key lessons learned from evaluations conducted in the Department.Consequently to that, a Senior Management Team (SMT) meeting was convened to outline the actions OCHA intends or has begun to take to translate lessons learned into practice.

OCHA has identified the importance of coordinated contextual analysis and needs assessments in providing an effective response to humanitarian crises.To further improve needs assessment and strong context analysis, OCHA has led the development of the Humanitarian Dashboard and coordinating efforts with other UN agencies.The Dashboard is a platform to consolidate, in real-time, and communicate humanitarian needs assessment and other key information from across sectors to better inform decision making.

Similarly, the SMT recognized that OCHA's humanitarian financing instruments have proven extremely valuable in allocating resources, but can be further enhanced with proper review of needs and existing local capacities.

Having acknowledged that strong leadership remains an important aspect of humanitarian response and that in some responses during 2010 OCHA was not able to deploy experienced leaders or there were gaps in leadership, OCHA has recently taken the necessary steps to ensure strong and stable top leadership in Libya, and has begun developing a comprehensive human resources strategy to attract the right talent and skill sets needed.The strategy will be completed by the end of 2011.

In addition to better needs assessments, context analyses, and strong leadership, OCHA is working to create even preparedness among humanitarian actors.To address this, OCHA will pilot an approach measuring the impact of preparedness work on response outcomes.More specifically, OCHA will identify measurable deliverables more frequently and consistently.Preparedness also hinges on IM.Existing guidance hasn't been sufficiently disseminated and understood.In 2011, OCHA will use existing OCHA inter-agency policy and guidance to develop performance frameworks at the Country and Regional Office level.

The Cluster Evaluation Phase Two provided recommendations to further improve the implementation of the cluster approach.This is an important evaluation for OCHA, given its a critical role in the success of inter-cluster coordination.In line with the Guidelines for Management Response and Follow Up, a MRP was designed by OCHA's Senior Management Team (SMT), which reviewed the recommendations directed at OCHA with three roles guiding their decisions.

Title: Multilateral Humanitarian Aid As a Foreign Socio-Humanitarian Policy Tool in Britain
Snippet: The article proposes to single out socio-humanitarian cooperation as a separate foreign policy tool. It studies the case of the UK to demonstrate the synergy between conceptual approaches and their implementation in the national legislation in providing official development assistance (ODA) and humanitarian aid as the two integral parts of socio-humanitarian policy. The authors conclude that the shift in doctrinal priorities in the area, including the prioritisation of emergency aid and individual recipients (Afghanistan, certain African states) after 2020, is confirmed by the change in London's approaches towards UN humanitarian agencies, with the pace of cuts to humanitarian aid funds being faster than the government's stated targets. Based on statistical data from 2005‒2023, the authors distinguish two periods of the UK's multilateral socio-humanitarian policy: 2005‒2020 and 2020 ‒ to the present. The first period saw the growth in London's emergency response funding being in line with the overall growth in global humanitarian needs. In the second period, despite the dramatic increase in the funds requested by UN agencies and the general degradation of the global humanitarian situation (the humanitarian appeal of the UN's main coordination mechanism, the Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), increased from $39 bn in 2020 to $51.5 bn in 2023, with the number of people in dire need jumping from 98 million in 2020 to 230 million in 2023), UK deprioritised practically all channels of multilateral humanitarian funding. For the second period, we show the emphasis on food aid, along with a staggering (up to 85%) reduction in other funding areas, most notably in unearmarked contributions and CERF pledges. Such a change may be explained, on the one hand, by the deteriorating food security situation in key recipient countries and, on the other hand, by the politicisation of humanitarian assistance on the part of the UK.

Title: Nuancing the double and triple nexus: analyzing the potential for unintended, negative consequences
Snippet: Humanitarian, development, and peace actions are often funded and implemented in distinct ways, within unique operational paradigms, and by different actors. However, certain contexts require humanitarian, development, and peace actions in parallel, either geographically or temporally. Additionally, many circumstances require flexibility to shift between programming modalities due to changing contexts. Due to these realities, intergovernmental, governmental, and non-governmental agencies have called for a nexus approach which has had two distinct iterations, the humanitarian-development nexus and the humanitarian-development-peace nexus, the former emerging in literature and practice prior to the latter (ICVA 2017;OCHA n.d.;UNDP n.d.). Title: “Post-Non-Classical” or “Post-Neoclassical” Epistemology?
Snippet: The social and humanitarian sciences are dispersed and fragmented due to their disciplinary boundaries. Consequently, the completeness, integrity, complexity, and multidimensionality of social objects under study are not "addressed" by current cognitive processes [12, p. 21]. 

Philosophers employ figurative language to convey the epistemological, methodological, and psychological implications of contradictions and difficulties in a way that encourages a willingness to "look at the face of complexity without fear" [13]. In this context, contemporary philosophers emphasise other points of epistemological and methodological importance. 

For instance, V. Arshinov and B. Budanov posit that the structures of interdisciplinary understanding within the complexity paradigm are inherently uncertain. Among the various cognitive problems that emerge at this time, the "complexity problem formulation" occupies a distinctive position. It is characterised by a "complex logical" and "non-linear process" [4]. 

In their latest research, V. Arshinov and V. Budanov examine the phenomenon of complexity in the context of the formation of "quantum semiotics." Philosophers posit that a "conceptual character" endowed with the capacity to observe and comprehend complexity should be formed. Such a cognitive observer can be considered a perceiving subject "in the unity of cyber semiotic, synergetic and quantummechanical perspectives" [4, p. 67]. 

In such complexity, it is challenging to demonstrate a single epistemological and methodological position in their context in the philosophical approach to scientific rationality and epistemological features. Indeed, researchers have observed that searching for solutions to the abovementioned difficulties led to postnon-classicism and post-non-classical rationality. This process revealed the existence of multivariate ness. 

In particular, post-non-classicism ideas, as they have been formed in the social and humanitarian sciences, can be divided into three groups. The first group comprises scientific research activities that employ interdisciplinary and polyparadigmatic approaches. This approach selects system analysis (synergistic) as a methodological foundation. System analysis synthesises natural science, social, and humanitarian sciences. In this regard, philosophers have separately observed that V. Stepin established a "universal discourse" for the dialogue between natural science and humanitarian "cultures" [15].

Title: Synthesis, part of a Special Feature on Applied Research for Enhancing Human Well-Being and Environmental Stewardship: Using Complexity Thinking in Southern Africa Exploring the implications of critical complexity for the study of social- ecological systems.
Snippet: Morin (2008:33) critiques the former as a reaction to reductionism, which insists on a kind of holism that is "...never anything more than a plastic bag enveloping whatever it found any way it could, and...the more the totality becomes full, the emptier it becomes." Such holism is a strong form of constructivism that negates the need for a reliable ontology, as reality is described in terms of our knowledge thereof (Preiser 2012). Despite the strong opposition to reductionism inherent in this view, it is precisely such a strategy that is employed in reducing all ontology to epistemology (Preiser 2012). In contrast, those complexity theorists who assert that all complexity can be conceptualized and measured in some way adopt a simplifying approach that does not recognize the intangible nature of many emergent properties, for example, a sense of place of a particular area. From this perspective, emergence is a matter of finding the right rules and laws to define the extent of complexity at hand. The idea that all complexity can be formalized, for example, by expression in fractals and power laws, remains largely unquestioned. 

These conflicting positions reveal the difficulties in resolving the problem of reductionism in unambiguous terms. Indeed, it is arguable that this problem is the central dilemma in the study of complexity. Cilliers (2005b:261) articulates this dilemma as an inescapable "performative tension" within complexity. This performative tension results from the fact that a rigorous understanding of complexity is one that denies both total holism and total reductionism simultaneously; while still acknowledging that any description of a complex system necessarily performs some reduction of reality (Cilliers 2005b). Therefore, we do not consider a complexity perspective as being in opposition to reductionist research strategies, but rather as both transcending and including such strategies. Here, the study of complex phenomena is at best a postreductionist effort that is necessarily a critical position (Preiser 2012). This insight is central to what Preiser and Cilliers (2010) term "critical complexity." Critical complexity follows the logic of reductionism, with a simultaneous awareness of the choices made in reducing the system.

Title: Understanding sexual violence in armed conflict: cutting ourselves with Occam’s razor
Snippet: Global development expert Ben Ramalingam (2013) suggests that simplicity, i.e. reductionist philosophy (Occam's razor), underlies much of the aid world, adding up to 'a system where simplicity is repeatedly, consistently, and damagingly chosen over relevance and appropriateness ' (p. 125). The consequence of this approach is that the issue cannot be effectively addressed (Wieringa 1998), illustrated by '[g]ender [being] treated as a portable tool of analysis and empowerment that can be carried around in the back pockets of both international humanitarian and development staff' instead of a concept that should inform core understanding (Hyndman and de Alwis 2003, p. 212). Simplicity allows humanitarian actors not only relief from the obligation to investigate structural contexts that (re)produce the occurrence of sexual violence in conflict but also exemption from scrutiny in cases where actors are complicit in (re)producing these structural inequalities. 

This necessitates a paradigm shift from conventional simplicity thinking to complexity thinking-a way of looking at world problems where interconnectivities, dynamics, and complexities are recognised rather than avoided (Ramalingam 2013), and thus towards a more realistic understanding of the issue (Ramalingam et al. 2008). If humanitarians would engage with complexity thinking, Ramalingam (2013) argues, 'the right questions would be asked rather than the right solutions provided; and organisational learning would be fearless and tireless, characterised by co-evolving and learning with 'beneficiaries' rather than for them: the international humanitarian system would be 'as open to change on the inside as it was hungry for change outside" (p. 363). This requires (re)linking not only critical research to humanitarian policy (theory) but also theory to practice. That means that researchers have to be willing to fearlessly engage with feminist thinking and give 'gender' back its political and practical potential, by (re)visualising sexuality and the symbolic dimensions of sexual violence in armed conflict (Wieringa 1998).

The social and humanitarian sciences are dispersed and fragmented due to their disciplinary boundaries. Consequently, the completeness, integrity, complexity, and multidimensionality of social objects under study are not "addressed" by current cognitive processes [12, p. 21]. 

Philosophers employ figurative language to convey the epistemological, methodological, and psychological implications of contradictions and difficulties in a way that encourages a willingness to "look at the face of complexity without fear" [13]. In this context, contemporary philosophers emphasise other points of epistemological and methodological importance. 

For instance, V. Arshinov and B. Budanov posit that the structures of interdisciplinary understanding within the complexity paradigm are inherently uncertain. Among the various cognitive problems that emerge at this time, the "complexity problem formulation" occupies a distinctive position. It is characterised by a "complex logical" and "non-linear process" [4]. 

In their latest research, V. Arshinov and V. Budanov examine the phenomenon of complexity in the context of the formation of "quantum semiotics." Philosophers posit that a "conceptual character" endowed with the capacity to observe and comprehend complexity should be formed. Such a cognitive observer can be considered a perceiving subject "in the unity of cyber semiotic, synergetic and quantummechanical perspectives" [4, p. 67]. 

In such complexity, it is challenging to demonstrate a single epistemological and methodological position in their context in the philosophical approach to scientific rationality and epistemological features. Indeed, researchers have observed that searching for solutions to the abovementioned difficulties led to postnon-classicism and post-non-classical rationality. This process revealed the existence of multivariate ness. 

In particular, post-non-classicism ideas, as they have been formed in the social and humanitarian sciences, can be divided into three groups. The first group comprises scientific research activities that employ interdisciplinary and polyparadigmatic approaches. This approach selects system analysis (synergistic) as a methodological foundation. System analysis synthesises natural science, social, and humanitarian sciences. In this regard, philosophers have separately observed that V. Stepin established a "universal discourse" for the dialogue between natural science and humanitarian "cultures" [15].

Morin (2008:33) critiques the former as a reaction to reductionism, which insists on a kind of holism that is "...never anything more than a plastic bag enveloping whatever it found any way it could, and...the more the totality becomes full, the emptier it becomes." Such holism is a strong form of constructivism that negates the need for a reliable ontology, as reality is described in terms of our knowledge thereof (Preiser 2012). Despite the strong opposition to reductionism inherent in this view, it is precisely such a strategy that is employed in reducing all ontology to epistemology (Preiser 2012). In contrast, those complexity theorists who assert that all complexity can be conceptualized and measured in some way adopt a simplifying approach that does not recognize the intangible nature of many emergent properties, for example, a sense of place of a particular area. From this perspective, emergence is a matter of finding the right rules and laws to define the extent of complexity at hand. The idea that all complexity can be formalized, for example, by expression in fractals and power laws, remains largely unquestioned. 

These conflicting positions reveal the difficulties in resolving the problem of reductionism in unambiguous terms. Indeed, it is arguable that this problem is the central dilemma in the study of complexity. Cilliers (2005b:261) articulates this dilemma as an inescapable "performative tension" within complexity. This performative tension results from the fact that a rigorous understanding of complexity is one that denies both total holism and total reductionism simultaneously; while still acknowledging that any description of a complex system necessarily performs some reduction of reality (Cilliers 2005b). Therefore, we do not consider a complexity perspective as being in opposition to reductionist research strategies, but rather as both transcending and including such strategies. Here, the study of complex phenomena is at best a postreductionist effort that is necessarily a critical position (Preiser 2012). This insight is central to what Preiser and Cilliers (2010) term "critical complexity." Critical complexity follows the logic of reductionism, with a simultaneous awareness of the choices made in reducing the system.
